the nature of public attitudes towards wind farms is not a matter of 'communication problems' or 'backyard motives' but a matter of equity and fairness.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of public attitudes and their implications for planning wind power developments.
the nature of public attitudes and the role of equity and fairness in the implementation of wind power.
the question of what makes people accept or reject wind power.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
public support for wind power in Europe is strong, but that the implementation of wind power is hampered by the fact that the public does not accept the way wind power is implemented.
the implementation of wind power requires a careful assessment of the landscape impact of wind turbines.
public opposition to wind power is not caused by a 'not in my back yard' attitude but is a consequence of a lack of equity and fairness in the planning and implementation processes of wind power.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
public attitudes towards renewable energy are more about fairness than about the 'not in my back yard' syndrome.
the implementation of wind energy is more a matter of social justice than of communication.
public support for wind power is not a 'given'.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the nature of public attitudes is different from the way it is commonly assumed by planners and authorities.
the implementation of renewable energies requires a more profound and nuanced analysis of the attitudes towards wind power.
the implementation of wind farms is not a simple matter of 'communication'.
